name: Barbell Bench Press
instructions: Lie flat on the bench with eyes under the barbell.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Unrack the bar and lower it to mid-chest with control.
Press the bar back up to full arm extension.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
coachNote: Keep your feet flat on the floor and maintain a slight arch in your lower back for stability. Drive through your feet, not just your arms.
tips: Keep wrists stacked directly over your elbows.
Pull your shoulder blades together and down before unracking.
Control the descent — don't let the bar bounce off your chest.
commonMistakes: Flaring elbows out to 90 degrees, which stresses the shoulders.
Bouncing the bar off the chest instead of controlling it.
Lifting the hips off the bench.
benefits: Builds overall chest, shoulder, and triceps strength.
One of the most reliable exercises for upper-body pressing power.
Scales easily from beginner to advanced loads.
safetyNotes: Always use a spotter or safety pins when lifting near maximal weight.
Avoid locking out elbows aggressively at the top.
startingPosition: Lying on the bench, arms fully extended, bar directly above the chest.
endingPosition: Bar lowered to mid-chest with elbows at roughly a 45-degree angle.

name: Incline Barbell Bench Press
instructions: Set the bench to a 30-45 degree incline.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width and unrack it.
Lower the bar to your upper chest with control.
Press back up to full extension.
coachNote: A steeper incline shifts more emphasis to the front delts. Keep it around 30 degrees to keep the focus on the upper chest.
tips: Lower the bar to the upper chest, not the neck.
Keep your shoulder blades retracted throughout.
commonMistakes: Setting the bench too steep, turning it into a shoulder press.
Using too light a load and rushing the eccentric.
benefits: Targets the upper chest more than a flat press.
Builds pressing strength through a different angle.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter for heavy sets.
Avoid excessive arching of the lower back.
startingPosition: Seated on incline bench, bar racked above the upper chest.
endingPosition: Bar lowered to the upper chest, elbows at roughly 45 degrees.

name: Decline Barbell Bench Press
instructions: Secure legs on the decline bench and lie back.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width and unrack it.
Lower the bar to the lower chest.
Press back up to full extension.
coachNote: Have a spotter help you rack and unrack the bar since the decline position makes this awkward to do alone.
tips: Keep the movement controlled — decline reduces shoulder strain but not risk from dropped weight.
Focus on squeezing the lower chest at the top.
commonMistakes: Using excessive weight because the range of motion feels shorter.
Rushing the unrack/rerack.
benefits: Emphasizes the lower chest fibers.
Reduces shoulder joint stress compared to flat press for some lifters.
safetyNotes: Always have a spotter for decline pressing.
Secure your legs properly before starting.
startingPosition: Lying on decline bench, bar racked above the chest.
endingPosition: Bar lowered to the lower chest.

name: Dumbbell Bench Press
instructions: Lie on a flat bench holding a dumbbell in each hand at chest level.
Press both dumbbells up until arms are extended.
Lower with control back to chest level.
Repeat for the desired reps.
coachNote: Dumbbells allow a deeper stretch and more natural joint path than a barbell — good for lifters with shoulder discomfort on barbell presses.
tips: Keep the dumbbells at a slight angle, not perfectly parallel.
Don't let the dumbbells drift too far apart at the top.
commonMistakes: Flaring elbows too wide.
Using momentum to bounce the dumbbells at the bottom.
benefits: Greater range of motion than barbell pressing.
Trains each side independently, reducing strength imbalances.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter or lighter weight when learning the get-up/get-down with dumbbells.
Keep wrists neutral.
startingPosition: Dumbbells held at chest level, elbows bent.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended above the chest.

name: Incline Dumbbell Bench Press
instructions: Set bench to 30-45 degree incline and sit with a dumbbell in each hand.
Press dumbbells up until arms are extended.
Lower with control to chest level.
Repeat.
coachNote: This is one of the most effective upper-chest builders — prioritize control over load.
tips: Keep the incline moderate to avoid shifting too much load to the shoulders.
Squeeze at the top without banging the dumbbells together.
commonMistakes: Bench angle set too steep.
Partial range of motion.
benefits: Strong upper chest emphasis.
Joint-friendly compared to barbell version.
safetyNotes: Get dumbbells into position with knees first, not from the floor.
Use a weight you can control through full range.
startingPosition: Seated on incline bench, dumbbells at shoulder level.
endingPosition: Arms extended above the upper chest.

name: Decline Dumbbell Bench Press
instructions: Secure legs on a decline bench holding dumbbells at chest level.
Press dumbbells up until arms are extended.
Lower with control back to chest level.
coachNote: Have a training partner hand you the dumbbells once you're set on the decline bench.
tips: Keep core braced since the decline position can strain the lower back if loose.
Focus on the lower chest squeeze.
commonMistakes: Dropping weights too quickly at the bottom.
Legs not secured properly.
benefits: Targets lower chest fibers.
Independent arm control reduces imbalance.
safetyNotes: Have a spotter hand off dumbbells.
Don't attempt heavy loads until comfortable with the setup.
startingPosition: Dumbbells at chest level on decline bench.
endingPosition: Arms extended above the lower chest.

name: Dumbbell Fly
instructions: Lie on a flat bench holding dumbbells above the chest with a slight elbow bend.
Lower the dumbbells out to the sides in an arc until you feel a stretch.
Bring the dumbbells back together over the chest.
Repeat.
coachNote: Keep the elbow bend constant throughout — this is a hinge at the shoulder, not the elbow.
tips: Don't go so low that you strain the shoulder joint.
Think 'hugging a tree' as the motion pattern.
commonMistakes: Turning it into a press by bending the elbows more at the bottom.
Using too much weight, which limits range of motion.
benefits: Isolates the chest without triceps assistance.
Improves the mind-muscle connection to the pecs.
safetyNotes: Avoid excessive depth if you feel shoulder strain.
Start light to learn the arc pattern.
startingPosition: Dumbbells above chest, slight bend in elbows.
endingPosition: Arms out to the sides at chest height.

name: Incline Dumbbell Fly
instructions: Set bench to 30 degree incline and lie back with dumbbells above the chest.
Lower dumbbells out to the sides with a slight elbow bend.
Bring them back together over the chest.
coachNote: Keep the incline low — anything past 30-45 degrees shifts the emphasis away from the chest.
tips: Move slowly through the stretch.
Keep shoulder blades pinned to the bench.
commonMistakes: Bench set too steep.
Rushing the eccentric portion.
benefits: Targets upper chest with an isolation pattern.
Good stretch-focused hypertrophy exercise.
safetyNotes: Use light-to-moderate weight — flys are not a heavy-load movement.
Stop the stretch before shoulder discomfort.
startingPosition: Dumbbells above chest on incline bench.
endingPosition: Arms out to the sides at chest height.

name: Cable Fly (Standing)
instructions: Set both cable pulleys to chest height and grab a handle in each hand.
Step forward with a slight forward lean and arms extended out to the sides.
Bring your hands together in front of your chest.
Return with control.
coachNote: Cables keep constant tension on the chest throughout the movement, unlike dumbbells which lose tension at the top.
tips: Keep a slight bend in the elbows throughout.
Squeeze and hold briefly at full contraction.
commonMistakes: Using the arms to press rather than the chest to pull.
Standing too far back or forward from the machine.
benefits: Constant tension throughout the full range of motion.
Easy to adjust angle by changing pulley height.
safetyNotes: Maintain a stable staggered stance.
Avoid overstretching the shoulder at the start position.
startingPosition: Arms extended out to the sides at chest height, slight forward lean.
endingPosition: Hands together in front of the chest.

name: Cable Crossover (High to Low)
instructions: Set both pulleys to the highest position and grab a handle in each hand.
Step forward and pull the handles down and across the body to waist height.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: This angle emphasizes the lower chest — pair it with the low-to-high version for full coverage.
tips: Cross the hands slightly at the bottom for a stronger contraction.
Keep elbows slightly bent throughout.
commonMistakes: Using momentum instead of controlled contraction.
Standing too upright, which reduces the stretch.
benefits: Emphasizes lower chest fibers.
Great finisher exercise for chest hypertrophy.
safetyNotes: Don't overextend the shoulders at the top of the stretch.
Keep a stable split stance.
startingPosition: Arms raised out to the sides at the high pulley position.
endingPosition: Hands crossed in front of the waist.

name: Cable Crossover (Low to High)
instructions: Set both pulleys to the lowest position and grab a handle in each hand.
Pull the handles up and across the body to shoulder height.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: This angle emphasizes the upper chest — the opposite of the high-to-low crossover.
tips: Lead with the hands, not the shoulders.
Keep a consistent, controlled tempo.
commonMistakes: Using back or shoulder momentum to swing the weight up.
Cutting the range of motion short.
benefits: Targets upper chest fibers with constant cable tension.
Complements the high-to-low variation for full development.
safetyNotes: Avoid locking out the elbows aggressively at the top.
Keep footing stable throughout.
startingPosition: Arms down at the low pulley position.
endingPosition: Hands together at shoulder height.

name: Pec Deck Machine Fly
instructions: Sit in the pec deck machine with back flat against the pad.
Grip the handles or place forearms on the pads.
Bring the handles together in front of the chest.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A great beginner-friendly isolation move since the machine controls the movement path for you.
tips: Keep shoulder blades pressed into the pad throughout.
Pause briefly at full contraction.
commonMistakes: Letting the shoulders roll forward at the start.
Using too much weight and relying on momentum.
benefits: Very beginner-friendly with a fixed, safe path.
Good chest isolation without stabilizer demand.
safetyNotes: Adjust seat height so handles align with chest level.
Avoid excessive stretch at the back position.
startingPosition: Arms out to the sides, elbows bent, forearms on pads.
endingPosition: Handles/pads brought together in front of the chest.

name: Chest Press Machine
instructions: Sit in the machine with back flat against the pad and handles at chest height.
Press the handles forward until arms are extended.
Return with control back to chest level.
coachNote: A good option for beginners learning pressing mechanics, or for lifters training around a shoulder issue.
tips: Adjust seat height so handles line up with mid-chest.
Keep wrists neutral throughout the press.
commonMistakes: Seat set too high or low, changing the pressing angle unintentionally.
Locking elbows out hard at the top.
benefits: Stable, guided path reduces stabilizer demand.
Easy to progressively overload with the weight stack.
safetyNotes: Check seat and handle position before loading heavy.
Avoid flaring elbows excessively.
startingPosition: Handles at chest level, elbows bent.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended forward.

name: Smith Machine Bench Press
instructions: Position a bench under the Smith machine bar.
Lie back and grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Unrack, lower to chest, then press back up.
Re-rack by twisting the bar into the hooks.
coachNote: The fixed bar path makes this a good option for training close to failure safely without a spotter.
tips: Position the bench so the bar lines up over your chest, not your face.
Keep the twisting motion controlled when racking.
commonMistakes: Bench misaligned with the bar path.
Forgetting to twist to lock the bar before letting go.
benefits: Allows safe near-failure training without a spotter.
Fixed path reduces stabilization demand.
safetyNotes: Confirm the safety hooks are set correctly before starting.
Double check the bar is locked before releasing it.
startingPosition: Bar racked above the chest, lying on the bench.
endingPosition: Bar lowered to mid-chest.

name: Push-Up
instructions: Start in a plank position with hands slightly wider than shoulders.
Lower your body until chest nearly touches the floor.
Press back up to the starting position.
Keep your body in a straight line throughout.
coachNote: The foundational bodyweight pressing movement — master this before progressing to weighted variations.
tips: Keep core braced to avoid sagging hips.
Point elbows back at roughly 45 degrees, not straight out.
commonMistakes: Letting hips sag or pike up.
Partial range of motion.
benefits: No equipment needed.
Builds functional pressing strength and core stability.
safetyNotes: Scale to an incline push-up if full range is too difficult.
Keep neck neutral, don't crane forward.
startingPosition: Plank position, arms extended, hands under shoulders.
endingPosition: Chest close to the floor, elbows bent.

name: Incline Push-Up
instructions: Place hands on an elevated surface such as a bench.
Walk feet back into a plank position.
Lower chest toward the surface, then press back up.
coachNote: A great regression for beginners not yet ready for full push-ups — higher surfaces make it easier.
tips: Keep the body in a straight line.
Lower the incline height gradually as you get stronger.
commonMistakes: Hips sagging.
Surface too low for current strength level, breaking form.
benefits: Scalable difficulty by adjusting surface height.
Reduces load on the chest and shoulders compared to a standard push-up.
safetyNotes: Make sure the elevated surface is stable before starting.
Keep wrists aligned under shoulders.
startingPosition: Hands on elevated surface, body in a straight line.
endingPosition: Chest close to the elevated surface.

name: Decline Push-Up
instructions: Place feet on an elevated surface and hands on the floor.
Lower chest toward the floor.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: Elevating the feet increases the load on the chest and shoulders compared to a standard push-up.
tips: Keep core tight to avoid hip sag with the added leverage.
Keep hands slightly wider than shoulder-width.
commonMistakes: Feet placed too high before building enough strength.
Losing the straight body line under increased load.
benefits: Increases difficulty without needing added weight.
Shifts emphasis slightly toward the upper chest.
safetyNotes: Choose a stable elevated surface.
Progress the foot height gradually.
startingPosition: Feet elevated, hands on floor, body in a straight line.
endingPosition: Chest close to the floor.

name: Diamond Push-Up
instructions: Form a diamond shape with your thumbs and index fingers on the floor.
Lower your chest toward your hands, keeping elbows close to your body.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: This shifts more load onto the triceps while still working the chest — good accessory for pressing strength.
tips: Keep elbows tucked close rather than flared.
Maintain a straight body line throughout.
commonMistakes: Elbows flaring out wide, reducing the triceps emphasis.
Sagging hips.
benefits: Increases triceps and inner chest involvement.
No equipment required.
safetyNotes: Build up standard push-up strength first.
Stop if wrist discomfort occurs — widen hand position slightly.
startingPosition: Plank position, hands together forming a diamond shape.
endingPosition: Chest close to hands, elbows bent close to body.

name: Weighted Push-Up
instructions: Have a partner place a weight plate on your upper back, or wear a weighted vest.
Perform a push-up as normal, lowering chest to the floor.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: Only progress to loaded push-ups once bodyweight push-ups are easy for high reps.
tips: Keep the plate centered on the upper back for balance.
Maintain the same strict form as a bodyweight push-up.
commonMistakes: Adding too much weight too soon, breaking form.
Plate placed too low on the back, causing instability.
benefits: Allows progressive overload on a bodyweight movement.
Builds pressing strength beyond bodyweight capacity.
safetyNotes: Have a partner assist with plate placement and removal.
Start with light added weight.
startingPosition: Plank position with weight plate on upper back.
endingPosition: Chest close to the floor.

name: Chest Dip
instructions: Grip the dip bars and lift yourself up with arms extended.
Lean your torso forward and lower your body until you feel a stretch in the chest.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: Leaning forward shifts emphasis to the chest; staying upright shifts it to the triceps.
tips: Keep the forward lean throughout the movement, not just at the bottom.
Control the descent rather than dropping.
commonMistakes: Staying too upright, turning it into a triceps-dominant movement.
Going too deep and straining the shoulder joint.
benefits: Strong compound chest and triceps builder.
Can be loaded with a weight belt as strength increases.
safetyNotes: Avoid excessive depth if you feel shoulder strain.
Build up shoulder mobility before adding weight.
startingPosition: Arms extended, supporting body weight on the bars.
endingPosition: Body lowered with a forward torso lean, chest stretched.

name: Landmine Press
instructions: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment or corner.
Hold the loaded end at shoulder height with one or both hands.
Press the bar up and forward until the arm is extended.
Return with control to shoulder height.
coachNote: A shoulder-friendly pressing option since the bar path naturally arcs, reducing strain on the joint.
tips: Brace your core to prevent excessive rotation if pressing single-arm.
Drive through the legs slightly for stability.
commonMistakes: Letting the torso twist excessively on single-arm reps.
Standing too close to the pivot point, limiting range.
benefits: Joint-friendly angle for pressing.
Trains core stability alongside the chest.
safetyNotes: Secure the barbell end firmly in the landmine attachment.
Start light to learn the bar path.
startingPosition: Bar held at shoulder height, standing in a staggered stance.
endingPosition: Arm extended forward and slightly upward.

name: Svend Press
instructions: Hold a weight plate between both palms at chest height.
Squeeze the plate firmly and press it straight out in front of you.
Bring it back to the chest with control.
Repeat, keeping constant inward pressure on the plate.
coachNote: Great as a warm-up or light finisher — the constant squeeze creates strong chest activation even with light weight.
tips: Keep elbows slightly flared for maximum chest tension.
Maintain constant pressure on the plate throughout, don't let it loosen.
commonMistakes: Using a plate too heavy to squeeze properly.
Losing plate pressure between reps.
benefits: Excellent for mind-muscle connection.
Low joint stress, good warm-up or finisher option.
safetyNotes: Use a plate with a comfortable grip diameter.
Keep constant control — don't let the plate slip.
startingPosition: Plate held between palms at chest height.
endingPosition: Arms extended straight out in front of the chest.

name: Single-Arm Cable Fly
instructions: Set the cable pulley to chest height and grip the handle with one hand.
Step forward into a staggered stance with a slight forward lean.
Pull the handle across the body until the hand reaches the midline.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: Training one side at a time helps correct strength imbalances and allows a deeper squeeze at the midline.
tips: Keep the non-working hand braced on the machine for stability.
Rotate the torso slightly into the contraction for a fuller squeeze.
commonMistakes: Using the whole body to swing the weight across.
Cutting the range of motion short.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Allows a stronger peak contraction than bilateral flys.
safetyNotes: Keep footing stable and braced throughout.
Avoid overstretching the shoulder at the start.
startingPosition: Arm extended out to the side at chest height.
endingPosition: Hand pulled across the body to the midline.

name: Resistance Band Chest Press
instructions: Anchor a resistance band behind you at chest height.
Hold a handle in each hand and step forward to create tension.
Press hands forward until arms are extended.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A useful travel or home option when no bench or machine is available — band tension increases as you press through the range.
tips: Step further from the anchor point to increase resistance.
Keep a slight forward lean for stability.
commonMistakes: Anchor point too low or too high, changing the intended angle.
Letting the band tension pull the arms back uncontrolled.
benefits: Portable, minimal equipment needed.
Adjustable resistance by changing band tension or stance distance.
safetyNotes: Inspect the band for wear or tears before use.
Ensure the anchor point is secure.
startingPosition: Handles at chest height, band under tension.
endingPosition: Arms extended forward.

name: Barbell Floor Press
instructions: Lie on the floor with knees bent and a barbell positioned above the chest.
Lower the bar until the upper arms touch the floor.
Press the bar back up to full extension.
Repeat.
coachNote: The floor limits range of motion at the bottom, which reduces shoulder strain and emphasizes lockout strength.
tips: Pause briefly when the upper arms touch the floor before pressing.
Keep the wrists stacked over the elbows.
commonMistakes: Bouncing the elbows off the floor instead of pausing.
Using leg drive excessively since the setup limits it naturally.
benefits: Reduces shoulder strain by limiting range of motion.
Builds strong lockout strength for the top portion of the bench press.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter or safety setup for heavier loads.
Keep the descent controlled to protect the elbows.
startingPosition: Lying on the floor, bar held above the chest, knees bent.
endingPosition: Bar lowered until upper arms touch the floor.
